title: The trp operon: repressor and attenuator
summary: Change one thing in a bacterium that has plenty of tryptophan, say what happens to transcription, then watch the change travel along the arrows one hop at a time.

spec.story: A bacterium growing with plenty of tryptophan. The two switches on the trp operon are at work.

nodes.label: TrpR protein
nodes.note: TrpR also switches off its own gene. That is left out.

nodes.label: Tryptophan
nodes.note: The cell also makes tryptophan, which closes a loop. The dotted arrow marks the cut.

nodes.label: Terminator hairpin
nodes.note: The leader can take two shapes. Here it is one on or off switch.

edges.reason: Two tryptophan molecules bind the TrpR dimer and expose its DNA-binding site.
TrpR is a dimer that is inactive on its own, so only TrpR that exists can be switched on.
Active TrpR binds the operator, so RNA polymerase is kept off the promoter.
Attenuation samples tryptophan carried on tRNA, so charged tRNA follows the supply.
With plenty of Trp-tRNA the ribosome runs quickly through region 1 and covers region 2, so regions 3 and 4 pair into the terminator.
Polymerase that has started on the operon goes on to transcribe the trp genes.
The 3-4 hairpin and the run of U residues make the polymerase let go of the RNA.
The trp genes encode the enzymes that make tryptophan.

edges.notModelled: The enzymes make tryptophan, which closes a loop. It would settle between on and off, which four levels cannot show.

perturbations.label: Delete the attenuator in the leader
Stop tRNA being charged with tryptophan
